result:
A picture is supposedly worth a thousand words, so at that exchange rate you've handed me exactly one picture. I'll spend it on this one.

A man is asleep on a ferry. He's on one of those molded plastic benches bolted to the floor of the passenger lounge, and he's taken the seat at the end of the row so he can lean his head against the window. The glass is wet on the outside. Through it you can see grey water and grey sky, with a slightly darker line where they meet.

He's around sixty. He's wearing a navy wool coat that he clearly doesn't wear often, because the crease from the hanger still shows across the shoulders. His shoes have been polished recently by someone out of practice, and there's dried polish caught in the stitching.

On his lap is a white cardboard cake box tied with red-and-white string. This is the center of the picture. He is completely asleep, mouth a little open, and his right hand lies flat on top of the box with the fingers spread, the way you'd hold down papers in a wind. Two fingers of his left hand are hooked through the string. Whatever part of him is in charge of the box did not go to sleep with the rest.

Two rows behind him, a girl of about seven is kneeling backwards on her seat and looking straight into the lens. She's the only person in the frame who knows a picture is being taken.

That's the whole photograph, and I have most of my words left. Here is what they buy that the camera couldn't get.

The floor is vibrating. The lounge hums at a pitch you stop hearing after ten minutes and start feeling in your teeth, and the string on the box trembles with it. The room smells of diesel, wet coats, and coffee from a pot that has been scorching since the first crossing.

The ferry is forty minutes late because of fog at the far terminal. He doesn't know this, since he fell asleep before the announcement. He's been up since four. The cake was finished at one in the morning, and afterwards he didn't quite trust it out of his sight, so he sat in the kitchen with it for a while and then lay down on top of the covers in his clothes.

He made it himself. Anyone looking at the photograph would assume a bakery, and that's the picture's one lie. He bought the empty box from a bakery near his house, and the woman behind the counter threw in the string and showed him how to tie it so the knot sits on top and makes a handle. He practiced on the empty box.

It's a lemon cake, three layers, the fourth he's made this month. The first collapsed. The second was dry, and he ate it anyway over the course of a week, standing at the counter. The third was good, so he made the fourth exactly the same way, and it came out with a crack across the top that he has covered with more icing than the recipe calls for. The recipe is on an index card in his wife's handwriting. It includes the instruction "bake until done," which he has spent a month learning to read.

His daughter turns forty today. She has had this cake on most of her birthdays and has not asked for it this year, and he hasn't told her he's bringing it. He isn't sure whether it will be welcome or whether it will be too much, and he went back and forth about it through all four cakes. What settled it was the third one. He stood in the kitchen eating a slice and it tasted right, and he understood that he was now the only person who knew how to make it. That seemed like a poor state of affairs to leave uncorrected. The index card is in his coat pocket. He intends to give her that too.

The photographer is a student with a secondhand film camera who felt a bit guilty about photographing a stranger asleep and took only the one frame. She'll develop it in a few weeks and like it, mostly for the girl looking back at her. She'll title it something about commuters.

In about twenty minutes the ferry will bump against the dock, harder than it should, and the box will slide an inch. He'll wake up. Before his eyes open, the hand on top of the box will press down.

There is no such photograph, of course. I made it up, and making it up cost nothing extra. I think the exchange rate is wrong, or it only runs in one direction. A picture can show you the hand on the box. It has no way of showing you the second cake, eaten standing up.

message.reasoning:
I'm working from an open prompt: write whatever comes to mind, in up to 1000 words, with a distinct voice. I could go with an essay, a story, or a meditation, so I need to pick one and commit. I'm weighing a few concrete subjects, like the word "threshold" or the way maps distort, and I want to steer clear of cliché.

I'm weighing a few ways to write this open-ended piece: a tide table keeper, marginalia, an umbrella repairer, all of which feel a bit too familiar. Then a more playful angle comes up: since the prompt is a thousand words, and a picture is said to be worth that many, I could render one single image at that length.

I'm settling on a picture of a man asleep on a ferry deck in the rain, a cake box tied with string resting on his lap, one hand still on top of it. I'm also considering what words can add that the image can't, like the time that passed before and after, the smell, and whatever sits just outside the frame.

I'm picturing the ferry scene in detail now: a man asleep on an orange plastic bench, head against a wet window, the window showing the cold light outside.

I'm picturing the man's shoes next, polished recently by someone who doesn't usually polish shoes, with a bit of dried polish caught in the stitching. I'm also fixing the box in place: a white cardboard cake box tied with red-and-white string, and his right hand flat on top of it, fingers spread, as if holding down papers in wind.

I'm picturing the girl two rows back, kneeling backwards on her seat and staring straight into the lens, the only one in the scene who knows a photo is being taken. Her mother is just a blur beside her. Then I'm stepping back from the picture itself and noticing it covers less than half of what I'd planned to spend, so I'm looking at what the remaining words can carry.

The cake is a lemon one, the fourth he's made this week, and I'm picturing him checking the layers for crumbs through the box corners while the boat hums under him.

I'm wondering whether to mention the wife's handwriting on the recipe card, which hints at a loss without saying it outright. Then I'm thinking the cake's purpose could be his daughter's birthday, something her mother used to make every year, though I'd rather leave that understated.

I'm planning the leftover words around the photographer: maybe a student with a film camera who feels bad about photographing a sleeping man and never learns about the cake. The box in the picture would mislead a viewer, since it looks like it came from a bakery. He actually got it by asking at the bakery, where the woman tied the string for him.

I'm settling on the ending: the ferry bumps the dock and wakes him, and his hand presses down on the box before his eyes open. I'm also considering a short, honest line that admits I made up the photo, since that's something words can do.
